title: BEFORE GOD GAVE ISRAEL A KING, HE KEPT FINDING SHEPHERDS
paragraphs:
BEFORE GOD GAVE ISRAEL A KING, HE KEPT FINDING SHEPHERDS
Abel carried a lamb. Moses carried a staff. David walked out of a pasture. Then Jesus said something that made the entire pattern impossible to ignore: “I am the Good Shepherd.”
There is blood in the grass.
A brother is lying dead.
Another brother is walking away from the presence of God with innocent blood crying from the ground behind him.
And strangely, one of the first occupations Scripture ever pauses to identify is this:
Abel was a shepherd.
Not a warrior.
Not a king.
Not a priest standing inside a temple.
A shepherd.
Genesis 4:2 describes him in Hebrew as:
וַיְהִי־הֶבֶל רֹעֵה צֹאן
Vayehi-Hevel ro'eh tzon.
“And Abel was a keeper of sheep.”
The expression רֹעֵה צֹאן (ro'eh tzon) means one who tends, feeds, or shepherds a flock.
It seems like an ordinary detail.
Until you keep reading the Bible.
Because generations later, another man will be standing among sheep when God begins preparing him to confront Pharaoh.
Later still, a forgotten son will be called in from watching sheep and anointed king.
And centuries after that, outside Jerusalem, the Son of God will look into a world filled with wandering, wounded, hunted, spiritually dying people and declare:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
John 10:11.
And suddenly the pasture begins to feel much bigger.
Abel.
Moses.
David.
Jesus.
Different generations. Different circumstances. Different roles in redemptive history.
But there is a thread running through the fields.
And if you follow it far enough, it leads to a cross.
Maybe that is why this story matters so much to people like us.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to be sheep without admitting that we are lost.
We know how to smile while wandering.
We know how to post Bible verses while privately starving.
We know how to say, “God is good,” while secretly wondering whether He still wants anything to do with us.
We know how to sit in church with our hands raised while carrying something inside that we hope nobody ever discovers.
A secret.
A relapse.
A resentment.
An affair.
A hidden browser history.
A collapsing marriage.
A prayer life that disappeared months ago.
A heart that has become colder than we are willing to admit.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence a wandering sheep can ever believe is:
“I can find my own way back.”
Because sheep need a shepherd.
And Scripture keeps bringing us back to that image.
Abel appears near the beginning.

Genesis tells us that Abel brought “the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions,” and the LORD regarded Abel and his offering. His brother Cain became angry. God warned Cain about sin crouching at the door, but Cain eventually rose against Abel and killed him.
The shepherd became a victim of violence.
His blood entered the ground.
God said to Cain:
“The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground.”
Abel is not Jesus.
We should never force Scripture to say something it does not say.
But the New Testament itself places Abel's blood into a remarkable theological contrast with Christ.
Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, and “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.”
Think about that.
Abel's blood cries out from the ground after an act of injustice.
Then, at the center of history, another innocent man is murdered.
Jesus Christ.
But His blood speaks a better word.
Abel's blood exposes guilt.
Christ's blood provides atonement for the guilty.
Abel's death demands that evil be taken seriously.
Christ's death shows us both how seriously God takes evil and how astonishingly far His mercy goes to redeem sinners.
At Calvary, God does not pretend sin does not matter.
He reveals exactly how terrible it is.
And exactly how great His grace is.
That matters when you have done something you cannot undo.
Some people reading this have memories that still make their stomach turn.
You would give anything to go backward.
You wish you could unsend it.
Unsee it.
Undo it.
Unbetray them.
Unsay those words.
You have asked yourself whether God could possibly look at the person you became and still call you home.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
It tells you that the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
There is a difference.
Grace is not God pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace is God entering the scandal, bearing sin's judgment in the person of His Son, and writing redemption where we deserved condemnation.
Then the biblical story moves forward.
And eventually we find Moses.
Not in Pharaoh's palace.
Not commanding an army.
Not standing before the Red Sea.
We meet the future deliverer in Midian doing something surprisingly familiar.
Exodus 3:1 says:
וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ
Umosheh hayah ro'eh et-tzon Yitro.
“Now Moses was keeping the flock of Jethro…”
There is that Hebrew idea again.
רֹעֶה.
Ro'eh.
Shepherding.
Moses had once lived inside Pharaoh's world.
Then everything collapsed.
He killed an Egyptian.
His action became known.
Pharaoh sought to kill him.
Moses fled.
The man who had lived among royalty became a fugitive in the wilderness.
And there, far from the life he once knew, Moses tended somebody else's sheep.
Imagine the humiliation.
Yesterday, Egypt.
Today, sheep.
Yesterday, proximity to power.
Today, dust.
Perhaps Moses thought the important part of his life was over.
But Exodus 3 tells us that while Moses was shepherding the flock, he came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
And a bush burned without being consumed.
The wilderness Moses may have interpreted as exile became the location of divine encounter.
God called his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
And the runaway discovered something many wounded believers desperately need to remember:
Your wilderness is not proof that God has lost your address.
Moses had a past.
God knew it.
Moses had fears.
God heard them.
Moses had objections.
God answered them.
Moses felt inadequate.
God did not respond by telling Moses how extraordinary Moses was.
He gave Moses something infinitely better.
“I will be with you.”
That is where so much modern spirituality gets the story backward.
We keep trying to convince broken people that they are powerful enough.
Scripture gives us something better than self-confidence.
The presence of God.
Moses did not rescue Israel because he finally discovered his inner greatness.
God delivered Israel through an inadequate man who had to learn dependence upon the One who said, “I AM WHO I AM.”
And perhaps somebody reading this has been standing in Midian for years.
You thought you ruined your calling.
You thought your worst chapter became the title of your entire life.
You thought the failure was final.
You thought the wilderness meant abandonment.
But God has always known how to find people in wilderness places.
Then comes David.
When Samuel arrived at Bethlehem to anoint the king God had chosen, Jesse brought his sons before the prophet.
One after another.
Strong-looking men.
Impressive men.
Men who apparently looked kingly enough that Samuel himself initially assumed Eliab must be God's anointed.
But God said:
“Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature…”
Then came the devastatingly beautiful truth:
“For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
Eventually Samuel asked whether Jesse had any sons left.
There was one.
The youngest.
But he was not standing in the room.
He was keeping the sheep.
David was in the field while everyone else was at the ceremony.
Do not miss the ache inside that scene.
They gathered the family.
And apparently nobody thought David needed to be there.
Some people know that feeling.
Overlooked.
Uninvited.
Underestimated.
The person nobody expects much from.
The sibling who does not measure up.
The believer whose past follows them into every room.
The person doing unseen work while somebody else receives the applause.
But God knew where David was.
The pasture did not hide him from God.
Samuel said, in effect, send for him.
David came.
And the LORD said:
“Arise, anoint him, for this is he.”
The shepherd boy was anointed king.
Later David would write one of the most beloved opening lines in all Scripture:
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
YHWH ro'i, lo echsar.
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
Psalm 23:1.
David understood shepherding from both sides.
He knew what it meant to guide sheep.
And he knew what it meant to desperately need God to guide him.
That second lesson would become painfully important.
Because David's story does not remain clean.
The shepherd becomes king.
The king becomes powerful.
And the powerful king eventually sees Bathsheba.
Desire becomes action.
Action becomes deception.
Deception becomes manipulation.
And manipulation ends with Uriah dead.
One of Scripture's great heroes becomes the center of a horrifying moral scandal.
The man who wrote about the Shepherd wandered.
Badly.
And Scripture does not airbrush him.
That is one reason you can trust the Bible's honesty.
It does not turn its heroes into plastic saints.
No amount of poetic language can make David's sin harmless. What he did was evil. Nathan confronted him. Consequences followed.
Yet when David was confronted, he did not ultimately save himself with public relations.
He confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a shattered man returning to God:
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love.”
Then:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
David had once defended sheep from predators.
Now David needed to be rescued from the predator that had risen inside his own heart.
And maybe that is where this article stopped being ancient history for you.
Because the greatest threat to your soul is not always outside you.
Sometimes it has your name.
Sometimes it knows your password.
Sometimes it uses your voice.
Sometimes the wolf is the desire you keep feeding while asking God to make it harmless.
Sin promises freedom and slowly teaches us how to wear chains.
And this is exactly why we need more than Abel.
More than Moses.
More than David.
We need the Shepherd none of them could ever fully be.
Then Jesus comes.
And in John 10 He does not merely say that He knows something about shepherding.
He says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
The Greek word ποιμήν (poimēn) means shepherd.
But Jesus does not stop with His identity.
He tells us what the Good Shepherd does.
ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τίθησιν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων.
Ho poimēn ho kalos tēn psychēn autou tithēsin hyper tōn probatōn.
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
John 10:11.
There it is.
The road out of the pasture leads to Calvary.
Jesus is not merely a motivational shepherd helping decent people become slightly better.
He lays down His life.
Why?
Because our problem is deeper than low self-esteem.
We have sinned.
We have wandered.
Isaiah had said centuries earlier:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way.”
But Isaiah continues with the shocking announcement that the LORD laid upon the suffering servant “the iniquity of us all.”
This is the Gospel.
The sheep wandered.
The Shepherd came.
The sheep deserved judgment.
The Shepherd laid down His life.
Jesus bore sin on the cross.
Then He rose from the dead.
The Shepherd who lays down His life is also the Shepherd who takes it up again.
Jesus says in John 10:18:
“I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again.”
Christianity does not end at a sealed tomb.
The Shepherd lives.
And because He lives, repentance is not a walk toward hopelessness.
It is a return to Someone.
Maybe you have wandered farther than you ever intended.
Come home.
Not because your sin does not matter.
Because Christ matters more.
Repentance is not saying, “I made a few mistakes.”
It is turning from sin toward God, trusting the crucified and risen Christ.
You cannot wash yourself clean enough to deserve Him.
You cannot perform enough religious acts to purchase forgiveness.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
That distinction must remain absolutely clear.
We do not support Gospel work so God will love us.
In Christ, we love and serve because He loved us first.
And when grace grips a person deeply enough, it does something to our hands.
We begin asking:
“How can I help someone else hear?”
Maybe that is why you found this today.
A Moses convinced his failure disqualified him.
A Cain standing dangerously close to a decision that will destroy something precious.
A wounded believer wandering quietly.
A skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely about religious people pretending to be better than everyone else.
Or a sheep who simply cannot remember the way home.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know the Shepherd still calls wandering people home.
Someone scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that grace still reaches real people in real ruins.
Because wandering rarely announces itself.
There may come a night when you need to read these words again and remember:
The Shepherd has not changed.
We want this community to be a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered unapologetically on Jesus Christ.
It does not make anyone a better Christian.
And it certainly does not buy salvation.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, gratefully, and for God's glory.
Because the point is not merely to build an audience.
It is to point people toward Jesus.
The algorithm cannot save anybody.
A ministry cannot save anybody.
A pastor cannot save anybody.
Jesus saves.
And that brings us back to the field.
Abel was a shepherd, and his blood cried from the ground.
Moses was shepherding when God called him from the wilderness to participate in Israel's deliverance.
David was called from the sheepfold to become king, only to discover that even a shepherd-king desperately needed the mercy and shepherding of God.
Then Jesus came.
Not merely another shepherd in the sequence.
Not merely another flawed man God would use.
Not merely another leader who would eventually need rescuing himself.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Son of God, the Good Shepherd who voluntarily laid down His life for His sheep and rose again.
And the New Testament gives Him another breathtaking shepherd title.
Hebrews 13:20 calls Jesus:
τὸν ποιμένα τῶν προβάτων τὸν μέγαν
ton poimena tōn probatōn ton megan.
“The great shepherd of the sheep.”
First Peter 5:4 calls Him:
ἀρχιποίμενος
archipoimēn.
The “Chief Shepherd.”
The pattern has reached the One who towers over every human shepherd.
And now the question is no longer merely whether you understand the pattern.
The question is:
Who is shepherding you?
Your appetite?
Your trauma?
Your ambition?
Your sexuality?
Your bitterness?
Your money?
Your need to be admired?
Your political tribe?
Your secret sin?
Your fear?
Your past?
Your own understanding?
Everyone follows something.
Jesus does not merely offer lost sheep directions.
He offers Himself.
He knows His sheep.
He calls them.
He leads them.
He lays down His life for them.
And He lives.
So if you have wandered, stop pretending the wilderness is home.
If you have sinned, stop decorating the chains.
If you have fallen, stop confusing your failure with God's final sentence.
If you are exhausted, stop believing you have to impress the Shepherd before He will hear your cry.
Turn to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Let His Word expose what needs exposing.
Let His grace heal what shame keeps reopening.
Let His truth confront what culture taught you to excuse.
Let His Spirit produce what willpower never could.
And when you look backward at the wreckage of your story, remember that Christianity never asks you to call darkness light.
David's sin was still sin.
Moses' past was still real.
Abel's blood still cried from the ground.
The cross itself proves that evil is more serious than we want to believe.
But the empty tomb announces something scandalously beautiful:
Sin does not get the last word for the one who belongs to Christ.
Shame does not get the last word.
Your worst chapter does not get the last word.
The grave does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
So share this with somebody who has forgotten the Shepherd's voice.
Leave the honest comment you almost decided not to leave.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is standing in a field they never planned to enter, carrying a past they cannot repair, wondering whether God could possibly still know their name.
He does.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth running through all these fields is this:
The sheep may have forgotten the way home, but the Shepherd has never forgotten the sheep.
